10316-roy-blakeley-s-adventures-in-camp:
Percy Keese Fitzhugh published this Boy Scout story in 1920, with Roy Blakeley as its cheerful narrator. Roy tells how his patrol got started, found a paper, and made for Temple Camp on the Hudson. The book belongs to a series that praised scout craft, loyalty, and fun.

Skinny, a younger boy, seeks a merit badge, learns to swim, and joins rows on Black Lake, while storms and strange campers test the troop. Camp-fire talks and a talk with Bert Winton round out the tale. Readers get a warm, funny scout adventure, told in Roy's own breezy voice.
10904-frank-merriwell-s-nobility-or-the-:
Burt L. Standish published Frank Merriwell's Nobility, or The Tragedy of the Ocean Tramp, in Tip Top Weekly on April 22, 1899. The story opens as the tramp steamer Eagle leaves New York for Liverpool, with Yale students on the pier waving hands, hats, and handkerchiefs. On deck stand Frank Merriwell, Bruce Browning, Jack Diamond, Harry Rattleton, and their tutor.

Frank's scheme for Europe drives the tale, with a tragedy aboard the ocean tramp to follow. Standish writes the clean, plucky adventure that made Merriwell a hero to American boys. Readers get a classic dime-novel voyage, full of school spirit and sea danger.
12729-the-high-school-boys-in-summer-cam:
H. Irving Hancock's High School Boys in Summer Camp, or The Dick Prescott Six Training for the Gridley Eleven, follows Gridley boys to camp. Chapters run from the man in the four-quart hat and Dick and some high finance through a human mystery of the woods. Dave Darrin angry, Dick grappling in the dark, danger on the hoof and a mad stampede follow.

Visitors for the feast, a woodland discovery, a new trap, a hard prowler, Tag Mosher, a fix, an ambulance case, a training bout, ten minutes of daring, a big storm and Mr. Page's kind of father follow. Hancock writes brisk schoolboy adventure, mixing football training with woodland mystery. The book is a lively summer tale for boy readers.
13510-knots-splices-and-rope-work-a-prac:
A. Hyatt Verrill gives complete, simple directions for useful and ornamental knots in this practical treatise, with chapters on splicing, pointing, seizing, and serving. Adapted for travellers, campers, yachtsmen, boy scouts, and all who handle ropes, the book carries more than one hundred and fifty illustrations in its full edition.

A catspaw is tied by taking twists with a bight in each hand and throwing them over a hook, while the Blackwall hitch, simpler still, is a loop or cuckold's neck. Pointing a rope means whipping, unlaying, and twisting yarns into left-handed nettles, then combing them out. Verrill writes for hands, not theory, so a reader can make a knot that holds.
1573-frank-s-campaign-or-the-farm-and-th:
Horatio Alger's Civil War tale for boys follows Frank, a Rossville farm boy whose town hall war meeting opens the book. When his father goes to war, Frank must run the farm, win a prize, and prove himself at home, while letters from the camp remind him of the larger struggle.

Alger's moral is plain: industry, honesty, and pluck win the day, on the farm as in the camp. The story moves between harvest work and soldier life with brisk, didactic charm. It is a typical Alger book, earnest and hopeful, written to stir young readers to duty and effort.
19522-tom-slade-at-temple-camp:
Percy K. Fitzhugh wrote this Boy Scout tale of Tom Slade at Temple Camp, published in Wisconsin in the late nineteen teens with scout approval. Roy's sacrifice, Indian scout signs, Pee-Wee and Mary Temple, and a mascot's first coup open a summer of tracks, trailing, and good turns.

A roadside joke about gasoline and soda shows the boys' easy humor, even when a trip goes wrong. The book teaches scout craft through story, and it keeps the series' faith that a good turn, done quietly, matters more than praise.
21306-dick-o-the-fens-a-tale-of-the-grea:
Dick Winthorpe, the squire's son, watches his father plan to drain the Lincolnshire fen and reclaim it as farmland. George Manville Fenn sets the tale in the great eastern swamp, where many locals live by the marsh and want it left alone. When digging starts, trouble follows: houses torched, horses and cows maimed, men shot, even murder.

A constable called in takes a dislike to Dick and his friend Tom Tallington. He tries to pin the crimes on them; at times even Dick's father half believes it. Broad Fenland dialect colours the talk. Fenland birds, boats, and weather fill the spaces between the crimes.
21723-songs-of-the-cattle-trail-and-cow-:
John A. Lomax gathered these cowboy songs and poems for a 1919 Macmillan volume, with a foreword by William Lyon Phelps. Lomax had spent years collecting American ballads, backed by a Harvard fellowship for the work. He had already published a well-known book of cowboy songs. Here he turns to the verse men sang and recited on the cattle trail and in cow camps.

The pieces range from trail songs to comic and tender poems by cowboy poets. Lomax prints them as working folklore, the art of men whose lives were spent on horseback. The book helps keep a fading oral world on the page. It remains a rich source for anyone studying the songs of the American West.
21757-the-hot-swamp:
Eight hundred years before Christ, a Phoenician sea captain named Arkal sails from a Greek port in this Ballantyne romance of old Albion. His ship carries one mast, a great square sail, and fifty oars, with a horse's head at the prow. Phoenician traders pushed past the Pillars of Hercules to the Tin Isles and beyond, seeking tin, amber, and gold.

Arkal's voyage toward Britain drives the tale, into seas and lands strange to his crew. Ballantyne sets his seafaring skills to work on the ancient world. The hot swamp of the title waits in the northern mists. It is a bold change of scene for him: his usual sea tale dressed in the oldest clothes of trade.
23436-aladdin-or-the-wonderful-lamp:
John McLoughlin printed this picture book version of Aladdin and the wonderful lamp, in rhymed verse with coloured plates. A wizard finds poor Aladdin, moves a stone from a cavern mouth, and sends the youth below ground through unknown realms to fetch a lamp from its niche.

Fruits that prove to be pearls, diamonds, and rubies dazzle Aladdin as he gathers treasure, and back home the lamp's genie brings food at a cry. The verse stays simple and musical, each scene paired with a picture for young readers. Children will love the magic, the cave, and the genie, while grown readers will enjoy this plain, old fashioned telling of a tale known the world over.
23645-the-motor-maids-at-sunrise-camp:
Katherine Stokes sent her Motor Maids to the mountains in this 1914 volume of the series, with Billie Campbell and her friends trading the road for a summer camp. Miss Helen Campbell chaperones, and a camp doctor keeps order. Chapters on rules, table manners, and a bog walk set the tone of cheerful, well-run outdoor life.

The story deepens when the girls befriend Phoebe, a ragged mountain girl who has lived all her life in a cabin, known no mother, and never had a friend. Gypsy cooks, a comedy of errors, a warning, and an attack keep the plot moving, but the camp's real work is kindness: giving Phoebe food, rest, and a place among companions.
24418-the-quantum-jump:
Robert Wicks wrote this story, with pictures by Llewellyn, for Amazing Science Fiction Stories in October 1958. Its blurb sets the puzzle: Captain Brandon explored space's far reaches and reported back. He finds it disquieting that the far reaches know more about home than he does. Brandon gazes at the Milky Way through his canopy, trailing like a bridal veil across black space.

Below his scout-ship stretch the red deserts of Sirius Three, lit by two ice moons. He thinks of the sun, 52 trillion miles off, a pinpoint lost in the Milky Way's dazzle, and Earth a speck in orbit, nine light years away. Thirteen years have passed on Earth since they left, for the trip took four years. They were shut in Astro One with five other men, above all Colonel Towers. Readers get a pioneer, far from home.
2712-a-drift-from-redwood-camp:
Bret Harte tells of a man all Redwood Camp knew as shiftless and worthless, who entered camp carrying his effects in a red handkerchief on a long handled shovel. In a community of strong men with sullen virtues and fascinating vices, no one expected better of him.

When the terrible inundation of 1856 comes, he lazily drifts out of camp on a plank, and the drift becomes his story. Harte turns a ne'er do well into an unlikely hero, with irony and pity. The tale shows his gift for finding worth in the last man anyone would pick.
28105-a-learned-dissertation-on-dumpling:
This Augustan Reprint Society volume pairs two anonymous eighteenth-century jests on food. The first, A Learned Dissertation on Dumpling from 1726, treats the humble dumpling with mock learned gravity. The second, Pudding and Dumpling Burnt to Pot from 1727, answers it as a complete key to the first piece.

Samuel L. Macey supplies an introduction for the 1970 reprint, issued by the William Andrews Clark Memorial Library at the University of California, Los Angeles. Together the two pamphlets show how Augustan writers used fake scholarship to mock fashion, taste, and learned pride. The humour still lands for readers who enjoy Swift's age.
30330-high-dragon-bump:
Don Thompson tells High Dragon Bump, illustrated by Paul Orban. A short tale, its tagline warns that if it took reduction or torch hair, the Cirissins wanted a bump, with hokum, thistle, and gluck. A young and beautiful girl with blond hair and smooth skin the colour of creamed sweet potatoes floats in the middle of a room. Wayne Brighton drifts into it, her few clothes concealing nothing.

Wayne, apprehension changing to confusion, asks whether she is going to reduce him. She answers that the word is seduce, mister, since they told her reduce too, but they do not talk good. She thinks she is supposed to seduce him so he will tell them something, and then they will let her go. Wayne says they want him to get them a high dragon bump, a thing he never heard of, and does not even know what it is.
30648-an-ocean-tramp:
William McFee writes An Ocean Tramp, published in Garden City, New York, in 1924 by Doubleday, Page, copyrighted in 1921. Books by McFee listed in the front matter include Aliens, Captain Macedoine's Daughter, Casuals of the Sea, and Port Said Miscellany. A Heine epigraph opens the book: she was lovable and he loved her, but he was not lovable and she did not love him.

A preface to the 1921 edition notes that by a justifiable artistic device, the letter writer, the ocean tramp himself, drowns at sea. Neither author nor publisher guaranteed the book as cold fact, and disillusion was not deemed necessary at first. McFee blends sea letters, romance, and wandering life into a tramp's tale of ships and shores.
31452-roy-blakeley-in-the-haunted-camp:
Percy Keese Fitzhugh's Roy Blakeley in the Haunted Camp was published by Grosset and Dunlap with the approval of the Boy Scouts of America. It follows Roy Blakeley and his fellow scouts into a camp with a haunted reputation. Fitzhugh, author of the Tom Slade and Pee-Wee Harris books, illustrated here by R. Emmett Owen, builds the story around scout life: work, fun, and the rumors that grow up around a strange place.

The boys mingle fun with their work, as one illustration caption puts it, and the haunted camp gives their summer a mystery to solve. Written for young readers, the book teaches teamwork and courage through adventure rather than lecture. It is a cheerful entry in a long-running series that made scouting itself the hero of boys' fiction.
32045-the-boy-scouts-in-a-trapper-s-camp:
Thornton W. Burgess's boys' adventure story, published by the Penn Publishing Company in 1915 with drawings by F. A. Anderson, sends the Boy Scouts to a trapper's camp. Burgess, already known for The Boy Scouts of Woodcraft Camp and The Boy Scouts on Swift River, dedicated the book to W. H. T. and his three boys. Its contents promise winter camping, woodcraft, and trouble on the fur trails.

The chapters move from an interrupted dream and Pat's sight of white magic, through the Blue Tortoise Patrol, snow-shoes and fish, and life on the fur trails, to Christmas in Smugglers' Hollow. A deer yard, poachers, a silver fox, and a conference follow, with the camp of the poachers and the sale of a black fox near the close. Readers get a wholesome outdoor tale, where scouting skills, trapping lore, and fair play settle a conflict with poachers.
33382-penny-nichols-and-the-black-imp:
Joan Clark's Penny Nichols and the Black Imp, copyrighted in 1936, opens with a black imp, a mysterious package, and a threat, then follows Amy's trail behind a panel to a holdup. Its chapters move from an invitation to lunch and a bold move to a robbery, a studio, a visitor, and a missing workman. Clark writes for young readers who love a fast, girl-centered mystery.

Penny herself, sharp and brave, drives the tale, with clues that reward close attention. The book's pace is brisk, its Chicago setting vivid, and its villains suitably sly. For fans of series mysteries, Penny Nichols offers a lively, old-fashioned adventure, where a girl detective outwits grown-up crooks and saves the day.
33968-the-academy-boys-in-camp:
S. F. Spear wrote this boys' camp tale, published in London, Edinburgh, Dublin, and New York in 1909 by Thomas Nelson and Sons. Boys of Massillon Academy gather one June morning near term's end, and the roll-call opens a camp story. Chapters follow a costly yes, off for Whaleback, camp life, a swimming pool, a fog-storm, and a wreck.

Anemone Pool, a day of freedom, boys in a trap, an escape, missing boys, and a board on the Una carry the tale to tents down. Spear writes for boys who like camp, boats, and scrapes. The book remains a cheerful school camp story.
4116-christopher-columbus-and-the-new-wo:
Filson Young's complete biography of Christopher Columbus gathers the whole life, from the home in Genoa to the last voyage home in 1504. The road from Santa Fe to Huelva, walked with a sad heart and a small talking boy, opens the tale of hopes fallen to dust at La Rabida.

From there the narrative runs through first landfall, gold fever, conquest, chains at Cadiz, and final return. Young writes with sympathy and narrative sweep, never hiding the cost of discovery. Readers who want Columbus whole, in one long Victorian life, will find this the fullest single version.
4330-two-expeditions-into-the-interior-o:
Charles Sturt's complete account of his two expeditions into the interior of southern Australia joins both volumes in one text. The expeditions, made in 1828 to 1831, sought the sources of the inland rivers and recorded the soil, climate, and resources of New South Wales. Sturt's opening reflection on rivers frames the whole enterprise.

A river watched from its bank, he writes, shows only flood or drought, while its nature is learned at its source, among its feeders. The complete text lets readers follow both journeys without a break, from the first probes inland to the later surveys. It is the fullest form of a classic of Australian exploration.
5100-alaeddin-and-the-enchanted-lamp:
John Payne's Alaeddin and the Enchanted Lamp retells the Arabian Nights tale in verse and prose, introduced by a letter and a poem of exile and return. Twelve years earlier, on a dreary winter day of drifting snows, Payne fled the mean miseries of workday existence, slander, and hate into the dreamland of the Orient distance under Syrian skies.

There he gathered the rainbow remnants of old glory lingering in ancestral climes, far from modern lovelessness. Alaeddin's lamp, ring, and princess follow in that spirit of recovered wonder. Readers get a Victorian translation that treats the Eastern tale as poetry, not mere adventure, and as an escape into story itself.
57-aladdin-and-the-magic-lamp:
A poor tailor's idle son meets a stranger who claims to be his uncle. This retelling of Aladdin and the Magic Lamp follows the boy into a hidden cave of treasure. The stranger is in truth a magician after one lamp.

Aladdin keeps the lamp and finds a genie who grants his wishes. Riches, a palace, and a princess follow, but the magician returns to steal the prize. Cleverness and the lamp's power decide the contest. The tale remains a classic of the Arabian Nights tradition. Later stage and screen versions kept the lamp, the genie, and the magician's trick in memory.
6738-the-four-canadian-highwaymen-or-the:
Edmund Collins bases his tale on fact, as his preface insists: everyone in that part of Canada who is not deaf has heard of the gang at Markham Swamp. Literary friends, he jokes, will call the book blood and thunder. They will say he is on his way to the dogs. Yet those same friends tempted the public with dull books and found no buyers. Collins will not quarrel with them.

The highwaymen themselves rob, ride, and hide in the swamp, in a story told with the gusto of a fireside yarn. Danger, pursuit, and rough justice drive the plot. The Four Canadian Highwaymen is a bold, old-style Canadian adventure, founded on a legend locals still told.
7188-higher-lessons-in-english-a-work-on:
Alonzo Reed and Brainerd Kellogg built this schoolroom work on English grammar and composition around a visual method: sentence diagrams that lay out how words hang together. Their notes spell out the code. A heavy line marks the main clause, solid and dotted lines mark other links, and diagonal lines mark words set apart from the frame.

Pupils learn by drawing the shape of a sentence, so that subject, verb, and modifiers show their roles at a glance. The book joins grammar drill to composition, moving from parsing single sentences toward writing with care. Its plain, steady method made diagramming a familiar classroom tool, and this text preserves both the lessons and their drawn grammar.
9195-the-slave-of-the-lamp:
Henry Seton Merriman wrote this romance of spies, love, and revolution, set first in a Paris street once called Rue de l'Empire. Chapters move from tools and burdens to reunions, broken threads, and puppets worked by hidden hands. A clue, a night watch, and a retreat lead to foul play and a stricken hero.

Christian Vellacott, true to his cloth, stands at the center as foes close in. Merriman keeps the intrigue taut and the feeling honest. The novel still reads as a brisk tale of secret work and open hearts in a Europe of plots.
9203-a-rill-from-the-town-pump:
Hawthorne gives voice to the town pump itself in this Twice-Told Tales sketch, set at Essex and Washington Streets in Salem. Noon by the north clock, noon by the east, and high noon by hot sunbeams: the pump declares its manifold duties, imposed in perpetuity. It claims to be town treasurer, guardian of the town's best treasure, water itself.

It chairs the overseers of the poor, giving bountifully to paupers without tax, and heads the fire department. The pump's comic boast carries a civic moral. The sketch remains a beloved Hawthorne fancy, witty, humane, and full of Salem color.
9648-tip-lewis-and-his-lamp:
Pansy, pen name of Isabella Alden, wrote Tip Lewis and His Lamp, a Sunday-school tale of a ragged boy's conversion. The tale opens in a crowded Sunday school, where scholars sing Happy Land and a teacher's seat stands empty. Half a dozen dirty, barefoot boys fill a long seat by the door, bright and cunning of face, bent on a frolic. Tip Lewis, their like, soon finds a lamp for his path.

The story follows Tip from mischief to faith, as teachers, hymns, and small kindnesses light his way. Pansy writes with warmth for poor children. A reader gets a beloved old moral tale, where a lamp stands for conscience, and a rough boy learns to shine.
a-drift-from-redwood-camp:
Bret Harte tells of a man Redwood Camp never valued: shiftless, worthless, carrying all he owned in a red handkerchief on a shovel handle. In a camp of strong men with sullen virtues and fascinating vices, he had neither, and no one even made him the camp's fool. He drifted out of camp on a plank in the great flood of 1856.

The short tale follows what the flood and the years made of this nobody, and how the camp's judgment of him came to look small. Harte builds the story on reversal: the least of the camp carries its moral weight. His Redwood Camp, among the giant trees, is the setting of his most famous fiction, and this piece shares its economy and sting.
a-rill-from-the-town-pump: Nathaniel Hawthorne gives voice to a Salem town pump in this short sketch from Twice-Told Tales, set at the corner of Essex and Washington Streets. Speaking through its nose at high noon, the pump claims every town office at once. It calls itself treasurer guarding the town's best treasure, head of the fire department, physician to the board of health, and keeper of the peace. Its boast is that water, freely given, outdoes tax-funded charity for the pauper.
aladdin-and-the-magic-lamp:
Aladdin and the Magic Lamp is a folk tale told here in plain form, credited to no known author. Aladdin, the idle son of a poor tailor named Mustapha, is approached by a stranger claiming to be his uncle. The man is in truth an African magician. He dresses the boy finely, wins the mother's trust, and leads him to a hidden place between two mountains outside the city.

There the magician opens the earth to a buried treasure vault that only Aladdin may enter. Sent down the steps, the boy finds the magic lamp whose keeper can grant him wealth and power. The tale follows his rise, his marriage to a princess, and the magician's attempts to steal the lamp back. It is among the best-known stories of the Arabian Nights tradition.
alaeddin-and-the-enchanted-lamp:
John Payne translated Alaeddin and the Enchanted Lamp from a recently discovered Arabic text, printing the volume in London in 1901. Payne dedicates it to Sir Richard Burton, his fellow labourer in the Thousand and One Nights. His introduction explains that M. Zotenberg found Arabic manuscripts in Paris containing the missing tales. Payne's conviction about Galland's interpolations stood confirmed.

Alaeddin, the tailor's idle son, is trapped by a magician in a cave of treasure. A lamp and a ring, each with its jinn, raise him to wealth and a princess. Zein Ul Asnam and the King of the Jinn, the companion tale, sends a prince hunting statues in dreams. Payne renders both in his ornate literal style, with dense notes. The book closed his great translation project as a final, disputed treasure.
britannica-1911-crimp:
A crimp was an agent who supplied soldiers and sailors by kidnapping, drugging, decoying, or other illegal means. Such agents worked openly in the days of impressment. The word later covered anyone who supplied merchant seamen without a Board of Trade licence. It also covered the lodging-house keepers who preyed on sailors and often worked with crimps. The Merchant Shipping Act of 1894 set the legal line between lawful agents and crimps.

The act let port authorities licence and police sailors' lodging-houses and set penalties for abuse. It punished overcharging, the keeping back of seamen's effects, and soliciting. Officers could send a discharged seaman home and forward his wages for a small charge. The entry says these rules nearly killed crimping in the United Kingdom. In American ports, above all on the Pacific coast, state licensing and limits on blood-money cut the abuse down.
britannica-1911-damp:
Damp is a common Teutonic word for vapour or mist, kin to the German Dampf, steam, and so moisture in general. Its oldest sense lives on in the speech of coal-miners. Their firedamp is marsh gas, which, mixed with air and fired, leaves choke damp or after damp, carbon dioxide, behind. Black damp is a gathering of gases that will not support life or flame. White damp is sometimes used for carbon monoxide.

As a verb, damp means to stifle or check a movement. Damped vibrations are swings cut short instead of dying away on their own. The piano's dampers fall on the strings and stop their sound. A chimney damper, by narrowing the draught, slows the burning of a fire. One word thus runs from mine gas to music and the hearth. Each use keeps the core sense of something smothered or held down.
britannica-1911-hemp:
Hemp is the bast fibre of Cannabis sativa, an annual herb. Its name matches Dutch hennep and German Hanf. Greek kannabis and Latin cannabis are cognate. Many unrelated plants unfortunately share the name hemp. Sunn hemp, Manila hemp and Sisal hemp are different plants. New Zealand flax is neither flax nor hemp. Deccan hemp comes from Hibiscus cannabinus. Pité hemp comes from the American aloe. Bowstring hemp comes from Sansevieria zeylanica.

The true plant is dioecious, like its relative the hop. Male and female flowers grow on separate plants. The female grows taller with darker foliage. She ripens five to six weeks later than the male. Males are pulled and steeped like flax when ripe. Females stand until the seed is perfectly ripe. Seed feeds cage birds and feeds oil mills. Fibre preparation, manufacture and trade fill long sections. Medical uses of cannabis close the account.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-lamp:
The altar lamp burns continually before the tabernacle, commanded in the Old Testament as pure olive oil burning in the Tabernacle of the Testimony without the veil. The Church requires at least one lamp before the tabernacle. It serves as ornament, worship, mark of honour, reminder of Christ's presence, and profession of love. Mystically the light signifies Christ himself.

More lamps may burn before the Blessed Sacrament altar, always in uneven numbers: three, five, seven, or more. The lamp usually hangs by chain or rope before the tabernacle, high and clear of the altar steps, or from a side bracket within the sanctuary. Olive oil is prescribed as a symbol of purity, peace, and godliness, and leaving the Blessed Sacrament altar long without its light is a serious neglect.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-kemp:
John Kemp was a fifteenth-century cardinal, Archbishop of Canterbury, and Chancellor of England, more statesman than bishop. Born at Wye in Kent about 1380 and educated at Merton College, Oxford, he practiced as a church lawyer so successfully that in 1415 he became dean of the Court of Arches. He also became vicar-general to the Archbishop of Canterbury. Henry V used him on embassies.

Made Bishop of Rochester in 1419, then of Chichester and London in quick succession, he joined the council after Henry's death. He backed Beaufort against Gloucester and became Chancellor and Archbishop of York in 1426. He led the fruitless Arras embassy of 1433 and was made cardinal in 1439. He put down the Kentish rebellion as chancellor again in 1450 and was transferred to Canterbury in 1452. He remained the king's mainstay against the Yorkists until his death in 1454.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-of-fecam:
John of Fecamp was an eleventh-century Benedictine abbot and ascetic writer, called Jeannelin for his small stature. Born near Ravenna early in the century, he studied at Dijon under his fellow-countryman William, Abbot of St. Benignus, mastering all the sciences and especially medicine, in which Bernier counts him among the cleverest products of the monastic schools.

Following William to reform Fecamp, John served as prior until 1028, when William made him abbot and retired to Italy. He defended his house's privileges and accepted the abbacy of Dijon in 1052. He resigned it in 1056 under the double burden, and late in life pilgrimaged to the Holy Land, where Turks imprisoned him until 1076. For the widowed Empress Agnes, who placed herself under his guidance, he composed ascetical works on prayer, contemplation, the heavenly Jerusalem, widowhood, virginity, and almsgiving.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wilhelm-dieka:
Wilhelm Diekamp was a German historian born at Geldern in 1854 and dying at Rome on Christmas Day 1885. Soon after his birth his parents moved to Münster in Westphalia, where he studied from 1867 to 1872, then theology at Würzburg and Münster from 1872 to 1875. Uncertain of his priestly calling, he abandoned it for philology, graduating doctor of philosophy in 1877 with a dissertation on Widukind, the Saxon leader, in history and legend.

Excessive study brought grave lung disease, which did not spare him effort. Teaching in public schools at Münster, Arnsberg, and Aachen while developing his historical training, he produced as evidence his Lives of St Ludger in 1881. That year the Westphalian Historical Association entrusted him with continuing the Westphalian Charter Book. In 1882 he became privatdozent, unsalaried lecturer, in history at Münster academy, after a year at Vienna studying diplomatics under Sickel.
christopher-columbus-and-the-new-world-o:
Filson Young's Christopher Columbus and the New World of His Discovery is presented whole in this Complete volume, the full 1906 life in one file. Young wrote from Spanish and Italian documents, advised on seamanship by Lord Dunraven. His four parts carry the Admiral from The Inner Light to Towards the Sunset. Genoa and La Rabida form the discoverer. Palos and the landfall make him immortal. Espanola's fevers unmake him. A Spanish deathbed closes the account.

Inside, Young keeps one standard: Columbus judged as a seaman and a man, not a statue. The gifts to Guacanagari, the lombard fired through the Santa Maria, Mendez's canoe, and the last pleading letters are all given in full narrative. Readers taking the biography whole get the standard popular life of its generation. It is warm to its hero's vision, honest about his government, and clear on what the voyages demanded.
doe-osti-17030335-report-summarizing-str:
Argonne National Laboratory report ANL-AMMT-031, by Wei-Ying Chen, Jiaxuan Li, Srinivas Mantri, and colleagues, studies how radiation changes a printed stainless steel. The steel, grade 316H, was built by laser powder bed fusion, a layer by layer printing method. Samples were hit with ion beams that mimic neutron damage, some while helium was added and some while under load.

Damage showed up mainly as void swelling, tiny cavities that grow inside the metal. As built and stress relieved samples swelled more than solution annealed and cold worked ones across most heat and dose ranges. Wrought 316H swelled less than the printed as built forms. The team also built a new rig for irradiating samples under steady pull.
doe-osti-2584762-monitoring-home-electri:
Prateek Shrestha and Kim Trenbath of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory wrote technical report NREL/TP-5500-92393 in August 2025. The study monitors how homes use electricity, using secondary wireless meters rather than utility billing data. The devices, made by Copper Labs, pick up data broadcast by whole-home meters and relay it to a central server at minute resolution.

The analysis covers 17 homes in the Denver metro and Aspen regions of Colorado, paired with survey data on building features and equipment. Shrestha and Trenbath compare load patterns across homes with rooftop solar, electric versus gas heating, different occupant counts, and people working from home. Minute-level data reveals appliance cycles and brief usage spikes that hourly metering misses, pointing to peak load times and avoidable energy use.
doe-osti-3005957-assessment-of-deep-burn:
Argonne report ANL/NSE-25/37, dated July 31, 2025, asks how far once-through HALEU fuel can be pushed and what that does to fuel cost. E. Hoffman, A. M. Bachmann, and N. Stauff of Argonne wrote it with A. Cuadra and C. Lu of Brookhaven. The study contrasts fast and thermal reactors. In fast systems, a larger core and denser fuel can cut the enrichment a design needs. Burnup, size, and enrichment trade against each other in complex ways.

A literature review rates fuel and cladding options by readiness. Doped, large-grain uranium dioxide fuels such as Westinghouse's ADOPT are furthest along and already in commercial use. Mixed oxide fuel is mature abroad but still unlicensed in the United States. For cladding, chromium-coated zirconium alloys and HT9 steel lead the field. Cost tables in an appendix price transport and disposal routes for spent fuel and high-level waste.
doe-osti-3011002-characterization-of-tan:
A Tank 9H annulus sample was prepared and checked for Savannah River Mission Completion by Lawrence Oji and Hope Brown of the Savannah River lab. The work supports residual material inventory checks for the tank. Three vials reached the Shielded Cells in February 2025, each holding about 200 millilitres of annulus salt solution.

Each vial was filtered through 0.45 micron nylon membranes, and the filtrates were combined into about 600 millilitres of sample. Wet solids left on the filters totalled about 4.8 grams, drying to 2.1 grams after 72 hours in the cells. Ion chromatography found nitrate, nitrite, sulphate, phosphate, and oxalate above detection limits.
doe-osti-3022921-satellite-embedding-bas:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/TM-2026/4420, by Byeonghwa Jeong, Daniel Adams, Andrew Zimmer, and Marie Urban, attacks a gap in global population mapping. The laboratory's LandScan program estimates population building by building, but footprint data are missing or sparse across much of the world, leaving those regions unmapped at fine resolution.

The proposed fix reads satellite imagery directly. Combining Google Earth Engine satellite embeddings with a UNet computer vision model, the framework imputes population on a grid without needing footprints. Applied to Taiwan as a test case, it reached an R-squared of 0.89 with a root mean square error of 18.70, beating traditional machine learning baselines. It also corrected false positives in settlement data, recognizing uninhabited places that building-based layers wrongly mark as populated.
doe-osti-3023470-differential-privacy-in:
Kaustav Bhattacharjee, Kapil Duwadi, Alex A Anderson, and Alka Singh of Pacific Northwest National Laboratory document a privacy upgrade to the Grid Kitchen software in March 2026. Grid Kitchen prepares power grid feeder models for sharing, but feeder data can expose sensitive operating details. Simple anonymization has failed in other fields when outside data let attackers re-identify records.

The team added differential privacy, which gives formal mathematical guarantees, inside the model dehydration pipeline. Carefully calibrated noise is applied to sensitive attributes under settings users can configure. Worked examples show a Laplace mechanism at epsilon 0.5 and a Gaussian mechanism with sigma near 0.969 in a moderate privacy mode, shifting a peak loading value to 73.05 percent. Modes trade protection against how much analytical value the shared model keeps.
doe-osti-3024392-hybridization-assessmen:
Soumyadeep Nag, Luis Fernando Enriquez-Contreras, Bikash Poudel, Trevor Atkinson, and Mahesh Acharya of Idaho National Laboratory, with Kyle DeSomber and Kevin Harris of Pacific Northwest National Laboratory. They model a hybrid pumped storage design in INL/RPT-26-90192, dated September 2025. The system, called Trybrid, weds pumped hydro storage to batteries and solar generation, and the case study is the proposed Corral Summit plant.

This first part builds the power flow mathematics. Equations adjust battery power for conversion losses in each direction, direct current to alternating current and back, and set maximum charge and discharge currents after a loss adjustment factor. Open-circuit voltage and solar input enter the same bookkeeping. The point of the careful accounting is that a hybrid plant only delivers its promised flexibility if every conversion step is charged its real cost.
doe-osti-3025025-design-and-validation-o: Harsh environments got mechanically validated, and this DOE poster covers autonomous systems. The pages detail the design findings. The engineers get their data. The format was poster. The data were engineer. The autonomous were systems. The harsh were environments. The poster were format.
doe-osti-3362443-integrated-approach-to-:
F. Patrick McCluskey of the University of Maryland led this project under award DE-EE0009349, running from August 2021 to July 2025, with Sudip Mazumder and Arif Sarwat on the record. Solar plants fail most often in their supporting electronics, the inverters and module-level parts around the panels. The team built a non-destructive way to judge that gear health by fusing rich field data with machine learning, so owners can forecast failures before they cascade.

Synthetic datasets cut the bench testing needed to train those forecasts. Failure detective work fills much of the report: one case weighs over-voltage cratering, thermal runaway, and overcurrent as rival causes. Cross-sections cleared the wire bonds and die attach, while crater placement near the emitter bond pointed to overcurrent as the match.
doe-osti-3364305-final-technical-report-:
A final report from Auburn University closes DOE Early Career award DE-SC0021215, led by Bryan S. Beckingham in the Department of Chemical Engineering. The project studied how mixtures of dissolved species move through ion-containing polymer membranes. Such membranes sit at the heart of water treatment, fuel cells, and solar fuels devices, where they must pass wanted ions while holding back reaction products.

Single-solute movement was fairly well understood, but mixtures interact in tangled ways. The team synthesized membranes with varied ionic and neutral building blocks, then measured multi-solute diffusion with an in situ spectroscopic method that avoided older, laborious setups. Results tied membrane structure and water content to the mixture behavior that emerged. One applied study paired the membranes with a new catalyst and beat a commercial membrane's fuel cell performance.
doe-osti-3364916-resstock-measure-docume:
National Laboratory of the Rockies report NLR/TP-5500-96826, by Lixi Liu, Jeff Maguire, and Yingli Lou, documents the heat pump water heater upgrade in ResStock 2025 Release 1. A heat pump water heater moves heat from room air into the tank instead of making heat directly, cutting energy use sharply. The document specifies how that swap is represented inside the national housing model.

Parameter tables show most inputs set to automatic, letting OpenStudio-HPXML size capacity and backup heating from house characteristics. One default set covers a 50-gallon tank at 3.78 uniform energy factor. Usage bins, operating modes, and desuperheater options are each pinned down. Modelers auditing ResStock results can trace the upgrade's assumptions value by value, which is the document's purpose.
doe-osti-3703520-pumped-storage-hydropow:
A slide deck dated September 2, 2026 extends the Rockies lab pumped storage cost model to running costs. Lindsay Ashworth of Small Hydro Consulting leads, with Stuart Cohen, Vignesh Ramasamy, and Evan Rosenlieb of the lab. No single source gives a full running cost for a new United States plant. The deck builds the estimate from five parts, each with its own source base.

Direct costs split into routine operations and major overhauls, which recur on cycles of ten to sixty years. Indirect costs cover overhead, insurance, and property taxes with federal fees. Staffing takes roughly half of routine direct cost in survey data. One long-used power-law equation gives a screening figure near nineteen dollars per kilowatt-year for a large plant. That sits close to reported averages for very large plants. The authors stress the figures suit screening only, and tax bills have no sound default.
doe-osti-3818602-anaerobic-digestion-in-:
A National Laboratory of the Rockies report dated June 2026 presents anaerobic digestion options for farms and communities in Puerto Rico. Eleven lab authors are printed, led by Andrew Bilich, Anelia Milbrandt, and Daniella Rough. The record is the Spanish translation of the study. Work ran with a Puerto Rican farm support centre in Yauco and the Hispanic Federation, under the Communities LEAP program. Small digesters turn manure and crop waste into biogas and fertilizer. For island farms, that means home-grown energy and less waste to haul.

The study walks through working island examples, then charts the technical, market, rule, and money paths for wider uptake. Permit rules ease for tiny sources: one site each in Peñuelas and Yauco stays under the island's small-source cap. The report aims to help the coalition pitch digestion as a self-reliance tool for Puerto Rican farms.
doe-osti-3914967-anaerobic-digestion-in-:
Ten staff at the National Laboratory of the Rockies, led by Andrew Bilich, Anelia Milbrandt, and Daniella Rough, wrote this September 2026 report, NLR/TP-6A20-95079, on anaerobic digestion in Puerto Rico. Digestion breaks down manure and other organic waste without air, and it yields biogas for energy plus a rich soil product.

Early chapters set out the island's weak spots: storm damage, costly fuel imports, and farms that need steady power. The report then explains how digesters work, gives real examples from farms and communities, and maps where new projects fit best. A long closing part walks through funding bids, permits, risks, and costs, so local groups can plan a project that has a fair chance to get built.
doe-osti-3914969-anaerobic-digestion-in-:
Spanish-language readers get the full text of the National Laboratory of the Rockies report on anaerobic digestion in Puerto Rico in this September 2026 edition, NLR/TP-6A20-98187. The same ten authors appear on the title page, from Andrew Bilich and Anelia Milbrandt through Thomas Hickey. The subject is farm and community digesters that turn organic waste into biogas and soil material.

The Spanish text follows the English report part by part. It covers the island's storm and energy risks, the basics of how digestion works, and cases from real sites. Long annexes list funding sources open to Puerto Rican projects, among them federal loan programs, the Puerto Rico Green Energy Trust, and local banks. The aim is to put the whole guide in the hands of the people most likely to build these projects.
frank-merriwell-s-nobility-or-the-traged:
Standish ships Frank Merriwell off to Europe in this Tip Top Weekly story of April 22, 1899. The tramp steamer Eagle sails from New York to Liverpool amid Yale cheers from the pier. Bruce Browning, Jack Diamond, Harry Rattleton, and a tutor share Frank's summer of study abroad.

Seasickness turns Rattleton into the voyage's comic sufferer. Frank solemnly recites a poem about a man who stepped on a banana peel and hasn't 'banana' where since. Diamond prescribes a sheet of writing paper worn across the breast against the sickness. Burt L. Standish keeps the ocean tramp's tragedy leavened with bunk-room humor.
frank-s-campaign-or-the-farm-and-the-cam:
Horatio Alger Jr opens Frank's Campaign at a war meeting in the town hall of Rossville, a farming town too small for lyceum lectures. The Civil War has come, Frank Fitch's father Henry Frost prepares to enlist, and fifteen-year-old Frank must run the farm and mortgage in his place. The subtitle names the exchange: the farm and the camp.

Letters from the absent father, read eagerly and answered even by little Charlie in his first epistolary effort, bind home and army together. Frank hires out, resists the squire's pressure on the mortgage, and keeps the family whole. Alger wrote the tale during the war itself for the boys who stayed home, and its patriotism is practical.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CampbellLouise-:
On March 14, 1964, the FBI wrote up a phone call from the press: Louise Campbell of Science magazine had questions. She was asking about neutron activation analysis, a laboratory method for measuring trace elements, and its use in the Oswald case.

The Bureau had applied the technique to evidence from the assassination, testing whether fragments could be chemically matched. Campbell's call shows the scientific press probing the investigation's laboratory work while the Warren Commission still sat. The memo is a small record of that contact, the Bureau noting a journalist's interest in its science, preserved as filed.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Classification_: nsia-Classification Clark William Kemp: the made public government document on the Clark classification matter, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item. From the archive shelves, for readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-KingCaseAffidav: Harold Weisberg swore an affidavit in the King case concerning incomplete Treasury records. Weisberg pursued the Martin Luther King assassination files as doggedly as the Kennedy files. An affidavit about records a department produced incompletely is a litigant's sworn complaint, filed to make a court act. The record gives the affiant and the subject but no date.
higher-lessons-in-english-a-work-on-engl:
Alonzo Reed and Brainerd Kellogg's Higher Lessons in English is a work on English grammar and composition, carrying their famous method to older pupils. The book makes the science of the language its subject, teaching grammar as a system to be understood, not merely as rules to be obeyed.

Like their Graded Lessons, it uses sentence diagrams, placing words on lines that show how each part relates to the whole. Composition lessons join the grammar, so that pupils learn to write as they learn to analyse. Teachers and historians of American schooling will recognise Higher Lessons as the advanced companion to the most influential grammar of its age.
knots-splices-and-rope-work-a-practical-:
A. Hyatt Verrill wrote this practical guide to knots, splices, and rope work. This second revised edition carries 156 pictures. Each picture shows how a knot, tie, or splice is formed and finished.

The first chapter explains kinds of rope, how rope is made, and its strength. The next moves to simple knots and bends. Later chapters cover splicing, pointing, seizing, and serving. Verrill wrote for travelers, campers, yachtsmen, and Boy Scouts, plus anyone else who handles rope. Clear steps matter more than theory throughout the manual. A beginner can follow one knot at a time and test each result.
nasa-tm-19680016347-target-pressure-and-:
A. B. Wenzel and Nestor Clough of Lewis Research Center report impact tests with explosively propelled projectiles in this 1968 memorandum. The shots were fired at General Motors Defense Research Laboratories under a NASA Lewis contract. Aluminum projectiles struck targets at about eleven kilometers per second, mimicking high-speed space debris impacts.

Five shots measured how peak shock pressure changed with depth in aluminum targets. Four shots measured crater sizes in stainless steel targets. A throw-off pellet technique supplied the pressure readings along the target axis. The team compared the new data with similar light-gas gun results. Such data help engineers design spacecraft shielding against fast impacts.
nasa-tm-19680023757-sounding-rocket-meas:
E. J. R. Maier of Goddard Space Flight Center reports sounding rocket measurements of the topside ionosphere in this paper. An ion mass spectrometer aboard the ARGO D-4 rocket measured ion makeup from 300 to 600 kilometers. The rocket launched from Wallops Island, Virginia, on October 6, 1966.

Oxygen ions formed the major constituent across the whole altitude range. Their share fell from over ninety-nine percent low down to most of the total at the top. Hydrogen and helium ions grew with altitude as minor constituents. Ion temperature rose steadily with height, while electron temperature jumped sharply in the middle range. Density profiles agreed well with ionosonde and Alouette II records.
roy-blakeley-s-adventures-in-camp: Percy Keese Fitzhugh wrote Roy Blakeley's Adventures in Camp, with pictures by Howard L. Hastings, dated 1920. Fitzhugh is named as author of Roy Blakeley, Tom Slade, Boy Scout, Tom Slade at Temple Camp, and Tom Slade with the Colors. The contents list chapters in Roy's own chatty style, each opening with the word Tells. Early chapters cover getting started, a visitor, a promise, and a paper Roy found.
the-four-canadian-highwaymen-or-the-robb:
Edmund Collins wrote The Four Canadian Highwaymen, a tale of the robbers of Markham Swamp, and owns in his preface that the tale rests on fact. Folk near Markham, he says, all knew the gang.

Collins grants that fine critics will call the book blood and thunder and damn his taste. He answers that a dull book does not pay, and a young writer needs bread as much as fame. Charles Reade, he notes, worked the same field for years. The tale gives a young Canada its own crime saga: a swamp gang, bold raids, and the law's hard chase.
the-high-school-boys-in-summer-camp:
H. Irving Hancock wrote The High School Boys in Summer Camp, subtitled The Dick Prescott Six Training for the Gridley Eleven. Chapter titles include The Man in the Four-Quart-Hat, Dick Grapples in the Dark, Danger Comes on the Hoof, Fighting the Mad Stampede, and The Medical Examiner Talks Training. Chapter one opens with Dick Prescott giving a stranger directions.

Dick says the man sought will be found in the lobby of the Eagle Hotel or near the hotel on Main Street. Asked how the stranger will know Mr. Hibbert, Dick doubts the name yet points to a young man fresh from Europe whose trunks are pasted with labels. Camp training, woodland danger, and football hopes frame the summer tale.
the-slave-of-the-lamp:
Henry Seton Merriman's The Slave of the Lamp runs to twenty-eight chapters, its contents say. In the Rue St. Gingolphe opens and closes the list. Tools, puppets, and false metal appear early. A clue, a scent, and Bury Bluff follow. Greek and Greek meet at chapter twenty-two. The making of Christian Vellacott ends the book.

Chapter one explains its street's name. Not many years ago it was called the Rue de l'Empire, Merriman writes. Republics are proverbially sensitive, he observes. Once established, they grow morbidly desirous of obliterating a past in which no republic flourished. The street is therefore dedicated to St. Gingolphe today, he concludes. That renaming opens the tale in its renamed street.
tip-lewis-and-his-lamp:
Pansy, author of Ester Ried and Four Girls at Chautauqua, opens her story in a crowded Sabbath school room. Scholars have just sung Happy Land, and the superintendent walks the room finding teachers for classes left without them. A long seat near the door holds the Mission Class.

Half a dozen dirty, ragged, barefoot boys from a narrow back street kick their heels, pull hair, and laugh, plainly ready for a frolic. Their bright, wicked faces contrast with girls in white dresses and boys in snowy collars. Readers get a Sunday-school tale about reaching poor children whom respectable congregations overlook.
tom-slade-at-temple-camp: Percy K. Fitzhugh's Tom Slade at Temple Camp was published by Whitman at Racine, Wisconsin, copyrighted in 1917, with Boy Scouts of America approval. Fitzhugh also wrote the Roy Blakeley and Pee-Wee Harris books. Seventeen chapters are listed in the contents. Headings include Roy's sacrifice, Indian scout sign, Pee-Wee and Mary Temple, a good turn, a mystery, and tracks and trailing. The title pages and contents are what is shown in this record, so Fitzhugh's camp story itself does not appear.
two-expeditions-into-the-interior-of-sou:
Two Expeditions into the Interior of Southern Australia covers journeys of 1828 to 1831, with observations on the soil, climate, and resources of New South Wales. Volume one opens with a quotation from Sir William Temple about tracing a river to its source. The dedication letter, addressed to the Earl of Ripon, names no author on the pages shown.

The writer thanks Ripon for permission to dedicate the work, and explains its slow making. Exposure and anxiety during geographical research had left him almost totally deprived of sight for many months. Friends' casual help brought the volumes to completion. He asks indulgence for errors made under such conditions, and offers the results of the two expeditions to the public.
